# Rule Registration Mechanism

Every rule class generated by [[source-language/lpp|lpp]] is registered with the
Loci runtime through a **global static object** of type `Loci::register_rule<T>`.
This object's constructor runs at program startup — before `main` — and inserts the
rule into the [[program-lifecycle/global-rule-list|global_rule_list]].

## The Registration Pattern

```cpp
// Rule class definition (generated by lpp)
class my_rule : public Loci::pointwise_rule {
  // ... constructor, member variables, calculate() ...
} ;

// Registration object — one per rule class, at file scope
Loci::register_rule<my_rule> register_my_rule ;
```

The `register_rule<T>` constructor:
1. Instantiates `T` (the rule class) to extract its metadata via the constructor's
   `name_store` / `input` / `output` calls.
2. Constructs a `Loci::rule` descriptor from that metadata.
3. Appends the descriptor to `Loci::global_rule_list`.

This happens for every `.o` file linked into the executable, accumulating the
complete rule database before `main` starts.

## Conformance Requirement

A conforming runtime must ensure that:

- `global_rule_list` is fully populated before any call to `rule_db::add_rules`.
- The order of registration across translation units is **not** guaranteed. Rule
  implementations must not rely on relative registration order.
- Each `register_rule<T>` instantiation adds exactly one entry to `global_rule_list`.

## Module Loading

Rules provided by a shared library (Loci module) follow the same pattern. When
`Loci::load_module("name", rdb)` is called:

1. The shared library is loaded (`dlopen` or equivalent).
2. Its global initialisation runs, populating a module-local rule list.
3. `load_module` transfers those rules into the provided `rule_db`.

A conforming `load_module` implementation must complete all three steps atomically
from the caller's perspective — after the call returns, all module rules must be
visible in `rdb`.

## Relationship to `rule_db`

The `global_rule_list` is a raw list of all rules linked into the executable.
The application calls `rdb.add_rules(global_rule_list)` to transfer them into a
`rule_db` that the scheduler can query. This separation allows an application to
construct multiple `rule_db` instances with different rule subsets — though this is
uncommon.
